chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: The 2011 Room house band with Frank Wess, violin and bassoon
summary: In 1950 his sextet is house band in a Black hotel room where Nat Cole and George Shearing's first quintet play, using violin, flute and bassoon in the arrangements.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: In 1950, I got this group together to work in a room that was in a hotel in Washington. It was a Black hotel, and they had a room there called the 2011 Room. They brought in big people. Like, the Nat King Cole Trio played there, George Shearing's Quintet, and we were the house band. This band that I had was six pieces, or six musicians.

The drummer I grew up with, and I might have mentioned him before -- everybody calls him Dude Brown; his name is George Brown. George Brown played drums. Frank Wess played tenor, clarinet and flute. I had a violinist whose name was Addaway Robinson, a very promising violinist and musician, but I guess for economical reasons he never chose to stick around and fight it out like a lot of the rest of us did. On guitar and vocals I had a singer who was very good, played very good guitar and also sang -- his name was Norville Reed. And I had
a bassist who was later associated with Count Basie as well as Frank Wess; his name was Eddie Jones. Eddie Jones at that particular time was playing bassoon and bass.

We had some very unique arrangements, especially ballads and things, where we kind of combined a lot of these, at that particular time, strange instruments to Jazz, like violin, flute and bassoon -- those kind of things. Anyway, we got very good comments from all of the groups that came through. Nat Cole liked us very much, and the members of the George Shearing Quintet, really the first quintet that he had which was a very good group... He had Denzil Best and part of...
John Levy was the bassist. The vibraharpist was a girl...

Yeah, I think Marjorie Hyams. And Chuck Wayne was the guitarist. At that time, Oscar Moore had just left Nat Cole's group, and he was with his brother's group. They had aa group called The Four Blazers, that featured Charlie Rouse.

Anyway, it turned out to be a very enjoyable engagement that we had there. And we stayed there for quite a few months, up until they booked Billie Holiday in. And for some reason (I don't know exactly what; there was a reason given), Billie Holiday could not make the date. Well, everybody was
disappointed, of course, since Billie Holiday was a favorite among the Washington clientele, particularly in this particular club.
